1.title: Understand connectivity gaps
1.intro: Many communities lack affordable, reliable internet. Your work is to find where, why and what would fix it.
pts: Measure before you build: speed test at different times at 10 spots, noting device, place and time.
Causes of gaps: distance from fibre, cost per household, cost of devices, language and skills, power cuts.
Choose a first community and list who already serves it.
Write a need statement with numbers: households, current speed, target speed, monthly price they can pay.
Ask household heads what they pay now for mobile data and what they would pay for a home line; record the answers in a table.
Map the village on paper: mark homes, school, clinic and hall, find the nearest fibre or tower, and measure each distance in km.
Identify households with no device or no one who can set it up, and estimate how many need a loan device or training.
1.ex: A village of 300 households has 2 Mbps shared at peak. Target 25 Mbps at under 40 a month per home. Ten tests give 1.8, 2.1, 2.0, 1.9, 2.2, 2.0, 1.7, 2.3, 2.0 and 2.0 Mbps; the sum is 20.0, so the average is 2.0 Mbps. If all 300 homes shared that equally at peak, each would get under 0.01 Mbps.
1.act: Run speed tests at 10 spots and write a need statement.
1.std: Tests have times and devices recorded.

2.title: Know telecom and licensing rules
pts: The federal telecom regulator licenses radio spectrum and sets rules for carriers; unlicensed bands have power limits.
Tower and mast siting needs municipal and sometimes federal approval.
Customer privacy and emergency-call duties apply to service providers.
Rural and Indigenous community connectivity programmes have funding conditions; read them early.
Decide whether your service counts as a carrier or reseller under federal rules, and ask the regulator or a telecom adviser before you charge customers.
Keep a list of each funder's conditions: who can apply, matching funds, reporting dates, and what happens if you miss a target.
Check the provincial rule on pole access and rights of way before you hang cable on utility poles or dig along roads.
2.ex: Row: 'Use a radio link | federal spectrum rules | stay within licence-exempt limits | before install | equipment certificate'. Second row: 'Mount an antenna on a mast | municipal approval, possibly federal rules | check the provincial and municipal rule | before building | written approval on file'. Write the date you read each source.
2.act: Build a rules table for a small community network.

3.title: Design a network a community can run
pts: Choose last-mile type: fibre, fixed wireless, satellite backhaul with local Wi-Fi.
Plan backhaul capacity: households x peak use per household.
Plan power with batteries or solar for outages.
Document so local people can fix common faults.
Draw a map of the link route with each hop's length in km and a line-of-sight check for wireless hops, noting trees and hills.
Select equipment rated for local winter cold and summer heat, and keep one spare of each key part.
Size a battery: add up the watts the equipment draws, multiply by the hours of outage you want to cover, and add 20% margin.
3.ex: 100 households x 1.5 Mbps peak each = 150 Mbps if every home used its peak at once; with 3:1 sharing the backhaul needed is 150 / 3 = 50 Mbps. A site drawing 120 W that must run 6 hours needs 120 x 6 = 720 Wh; with 20% margin that is 720 x 1.2 = 864 Wh.
3.act: Draw a network plan and compute backhaul.

4.title: Cost it and set affordable prices
4.intro: Costs per household drive the model.
pts: Capital per household passed vs connected.
Monthly cost: backhaul, power, support, replacement fund.
Price tiers and community subsidy.
Payback and funding sources.
Separate the cost to pass a home (cable or signal reaches it) from the cost to connect it (drop line, router, labour), and budget both.
Offer a low-income tier or a shared-hotspot option and show who pays the difference, such as a community fund.
Run three take-up cases (40%, 60%, 80%) and find the case where monthly margin no longer covers monthly cost.
4.ex: Teaching figures in CAD. Build cost 4,200 for a site of 150 homes; monthly cost per household 25; price 35; margin 10 per home. If all 150 homes pay, margin is 10 x 150 = 1,500 a month. At 60% take-up, 150 homes become 90 paying homes, so margin is 90 x 10 = 900 a month. Payback on 4,200 is 4,200 / 900 = about 4.7 months.

5.title: Operate and support
pts: Monitor uptime and speed.
Local support person with a spare kit.
Response times published.
Track complaints.
Set up a monitor that checks each radio every 5 minutes and texts the support person when two checks in a row fail.
Keep a labelled spares box with a count, and reorder when any item falls to one.
Write a one-page fault guide: symptom, first check, fix, and when to call for help.
5.ex: Uptime 98%; fixed within 1 day in 90% of cases. A 30-day month has 720 hours, so 98% uptime allows 720 x 0.02 = 14.4 hours down. If there were 20 faults, 90% fixed within a day means 18 fixed in a day and 2 slower.

6.title: Train users and grow adoption
pts: Offer short classes in local languages.
Teach safe use, banking and learning platforms.
Partner with schools and libraries.
Measure use.
Build a short lesson plan for each skill, such as sending a message, joining a video call with a clinic or applying online, with a hands-on task and a 5-question check.
Train two local helpers and give them a printed guide, so help stays in the community.
Run classes at times suited to shift workers, elders and parents, and record attendance by group to see who is missing.
6.ex: After 8 classes, weekly users rose from 90 to 210. Weekly users rose by 210 - 90 = 120, or 120 / 90 = about 133%. Eight classes of 15 learners reached 8 x 15 = 120 people, which matches the gain.

7.title: Manage safety, privacy and equity
pts: Protect user data; do not read traffic.
Child-safety tools.
Fair access and pricing.
Climate and tower safety.
Write a privacy notice in plain words and local languages and give it to each new subscriber.
Offer a content filter for homes with children and explain that parents choose whether to use it.
Check the provincial rule on what you must hand over if police ask, and keep a record of any request.
7.ex: Policy: 'We log connection times for 30 days only.' With 150 homes making 20 connections a day, the log holds at most 150 x 20 x 30 = 90,000 entries before the oldest are deleted.

8.title: Pilot and sustain
pts: 90 days.
Measure take-up, uptime, satisfaction.
Stop rule: under 30% take-up after 90 days means redesign.
Plan sustainability.
Hold a review at day 30, 60 and 90 using the same four numbers: take-up, uptime, complaints, and money in versus money out.
Ask 10 subscribers and 10 non-subscribers why, and record the reasons in a table.
Write a handover plan: who owns the equipment, who collects fees, who keeps spares, and how the community votes on price changes.
8.ex: Take-up 46%. Of 150 homes, 46% take-up is 150 x 0.46 = 69 homes. The stop rule of 30% is 45 homes, so the pilot passes with 24 homes to spare.

quiz: Why test speed at different times?
Households times peak use, adjusted for sharing.
Access without skill does not create use.
Public connectivity programmes or a community fund; read each funder's conditions first.
